paper_title: $Ψ$-0.6: Adaptive Streams of Thought in a Unified Vision-Language World Model

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Humans reason about the physical world by flexibly combining different forms of inference as a problem unfolds. Achieving this flexibility is a major open challenge in AI: capabilities often remain separated across specialized models, limiting how they can be composed and jointly adapted to a task. We introduce $Ψ$-0.6, a unified vision-language world model that adaptively composes perception, language, geometry, and simulation within a shared reasoning process we call streams of thought. These streams interleave images, text, and explicit representations of geometry and motion, all of which the model can generate and interpret through a shared token interface. $Ψ$-0.6 surpasses leading open-weight models zero-shot on multi-view spatial reasoning, with further gains from reasoning through geometric intermediates. It also supports counterfactual simulation: generating and interpreting imagined scenes to determine, for example, whether moving an object would obstruct a pathway. Reinforcement learning from task feedback jointly optimizes the selection, generation, and use of intermediate representations, improving visual question-answering accuracy with gains that transfer to unseen benchmarks. $Ψ$-0.6 offers a path toward adaptive physical reasoning -- not only predicting the physical world but also choosing the representations through which to reason.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: Solving problem simply means representing it so as to make the solution transparent. Herbert A. Simon, The Sciences of the Artificial Humans reason flexibly about the physical world, shifting between different forms of inference as problem unfolds. When assembling furniture, we read instructions, change viewpoint, and mentally rotate panel to imagine whether it will fit. These abilities are remarkably powerful, in three related but distinct senses. First, they are unified: diverse capabilities are expressed in single system. Second, they are compositional: intermediate inferences and imagined states can be combined into solutions that no single operation provides. Third, they are adaptive: which representations are useful depends on the task, and experience can improve how they are selected and used. For example, words express goals and relations; geometric representations expose spatial structure; and imagined scenes reveal possible action consequences [1, 2]. Here we ask: how can an AI system learn which representations are useful for solving problems in the physical world? This remains major challenge for current physical AI systems, as capabilities often remain fragmented across specialized models, limiting how flexibly they can be combined and adapted to task. Vision encoders estimate and perceive, vision-language models (VLMs) describe and answer, and world models (WMs) predict and imagine each with separate architecture, training, and interface. This separation makes it difficult to compose these capabilities within shared reasoning process and jointly optimize how these models predictions are generated and used through downstream task feedback. growing body of work builds unified multimodal models [3, 4, 5, 6, 7], but these capabilities are not integrated into shared reasoning process. Another line of work allows language or vision-language models to invoke external models, tools, or programs [8, 9, 10]. However, the invoked components are typically treated as fixed black boxes whose prediction mechanisms are not jointly optimized with the reasoner for downstream tasks. *Equal contribution. Ψ-0.6: Adaptive Streams of Thought in Unified Vision-Language World Model Figure 1: Ψ-0.6: representation-adaptive reasoning across vision, language, and world modeling. (A) Capability unification. Diverse representations share common token interface. Different choices of supplied and predicted tokens express perception, geometry, language, and imagination within single transformer. (B) Compositional unification. Streams of thought combine model capabilities. (C) Optimization unification. Because intermediate representations are predictions of the same model, choosing which representations to generate and use becomes learnable action. To achieve flexible reasoning, we turn to powerful recipe that already exists in large language models (LLMs): (i) unified model provides broad repertoire of capabilities, (ii) generic 2 Ψ-0.6: Adaptive Streams of Thought in Unified Vision-Language World Model prompting interface makes those capabilities accessible and composable across tasks [11, 12], and (iii) reinforcement learning on task outcomes shapes the intermediate reasoning strategies used to solve problem [13]. Chain-of-thought has been central to the reasoning capabilities of modern LLMs, motivating the question of whether similarly self-directed, adaptive reasoning can extend to the physical world. Doing so requires making visual and geometric predictions available not only as task outputs, but as intermediate operations that model can generate, compose, and learn to use. We introduce Ψ-0.6, unified vision-language world model that adaptively composes perception, language, geometry, and simulation within shared reasoning process we call streams of thought. These are sequences interleaving images and text with explicit representations of geometry and motion  (Fig. 1)  . Ψ-0.6 builds on the Probabilistic Structure Integration (PSI; Ψ) framework [14], extending it to language and flexible reasoning. The model predicts images, text, camera pose, depth, optical flow, and point tracks as tokens with shared transformer. An any-to-any prompting interface allows it to condition on and generate these representations in different combinations, so the output of one operation can become context for the next (2.2). For example, an image pair can prompt camera-pose estimate, while an image and camera pose can prompt new view. Unification thus turns representations into reasoning operations: the same model can generate them, condition on them, compose them, and learn when they are useful. World modeling extends these streams beyond observed scenes through counterfactual simulation: asked whether moving an object would obstruct pathway, the model can translate the specified displacement into an optical-flow prediction, generate the resulting scene, and answer using its own prediction. Crucially, the reasoner and imaginer are the same model: predicted scenes are generated and interpreted within the same token interface rather than supplied by separate visual generator. Beyond prescribed reasoning pathways, Ψ-0.6 learns representation-adaptive streams of thought through reinforcement learning on task feedback. Because geometric intermediates, imagined views, and text are all actions of the same policy, downstream reward can shape both which representations are generated and their contents. Unlike VLMs that invoke fixed external tools, Ψ-0.6 generates these intermediates within the reasoner itself, enabling their generation and use to be jointly optimized end to end (6). Our experiments demonstrate three benefits of unification: strong zero-shot capabilities, compositional physical reasoning, and the ability to learn adaptive reasoning strategies from task feedback. On MindCube [15], challenging benchmark of multi-view spatial reasoning, Ψ-0.6 outperforms leading open-weight models in zero-shot evaluation, with further gains from geometric context and composed streams of thought (4). On FlowBench [16], when given specified counterfactual motion, its world-modeling capabilities surpass those of dedicated expert models that receive privileged inputs. In simulation, its performance on counterfactual questions comes close to that of other leading open-source VLMs, and it transfers to real robot data after training only on simulation examples (5). Reinforcement learning yields mean relative accuracy gains over video-only question-answering baseline on held-out data and across four unseen benchmarks, demonstrating transfer of the learned policy (6). Together, these results demonstrate our core thesis that unifying perception, geometry, language, and imagination allows task feedback to shape not only what model predicts but also how it reasons. 3 Ψ-0.6: Adaptive Streams of Thought in Unified Vision-Language World Model Figure 2: Architecture, training recipe, and prompting interface. (A) Ψ-0.6 is unified model across diverse modalities. Pretraining, mid-training, and post-training sample different sequence families; hollow tokens denote stochastically included sequence elements. Generic prompting interface: prompts specify the available information and requested inference pathway. Ψ-0.6 is interactive: it can generate view based on user-specified camera pose, then use that generated view as context for subsequent reasoning. (B) Fine-grained control: each patch is represented by pointer token and content tokens. Pointers specify modality and spatial and temporal locations, enabling targeted conditioning and scene edits. Probabilistic prediction: Ψ-0.6 represents distribution over compatible continuations, allowing the same prompt to yield alternative predictions through sampling.

sections.title: 2 A Unified Model with Adaptive Streams of Thought
sections.content: Ψ-0.6 combines three conceptual components, extending familiar LLM recipe beyond language: (i) unified model provides broad repertoire of visual, geometric, and linguistic capabilities; (ii) generic prompting interface flexibly accesses and composes these capabilities; and (iii) reinforcement learning teaches the model to direct its own reasoning from task feedback. Here we explain how these components support capability unification, compositional unification, and optimization unification, respectively. 4 Ψ-0.6: Adaptive Streams of Thought in Unified Vision-Language World Model

sections.title: 2.1 Unified Multimodal Model
sections.content: Architecture: one vocabulary, one transformer. Images, camera pose, depth, optical flow, point tracks, and text are serialized as tokens in sequence processed by our 8B-parameter autoregressive transformer. Perception, description, and simulation thus become different conditional predictions.

sections.title: 2.2 Generic Prompting Interface: Streams of Thought
sections.content: A generic prompting interface makes the models capabilities available as flexible reasoning operations. Ψ-0.6 reasons through streams of thought: sequences interleaving images and text with explicit visual abstractions, including camera pose, depth, optical flow, and point tracks. These representations offer complementary projections of the world, allowing each reasoning step to use representation suited to the problem text, geometry, or predicted scene. Any-to-any prompting: all tasks are token orderings. prompt specifies what is given and what is requested. Different token choices and orderings express different inference pathways through the same model. Any modality combination can condition prediction, enabling richly controllable world modeling over spatial, temporal, and semantic aspects of scene. Let RGB0 denote an image, while C01 and F01 denote camera motion and optical flow. Then RGB0, C01 RGB1 and RGB0, RGB1 C01 express novel view synthesis and pose estimation; replacing with gives motion-conditioned generation and flow estimation. These are conditional predictions of the same model. camera pose can therefore serve as an estimate when inferred from images, command when supplied to generate view, or an intermediate when used to answer spatial question. In this sense, the model acts as multiverse generator over garden of forking paths [17]. Prompts control both what is constrained and what is left for the model to infer. Compositional reasoning: predictions become context. Streams of thought compose these conditional predictions into multistep reasoning processes, with the output of one prediction providing context for the next. For example, the model can generate view from an image and user-specified camera pose, then use the generated view as context for answering spatial question (Fig. 2A). Visual and geometric predictions are therefore not only task outputs, but intermediate operations that connect perception, language, and imagination within one reasoning process. prompt can prescribe these operations; their selection can also become part of what the model learns. Ψ-0.6 builds on Probabilistic Structure Integration (PSI; Ψ) [14], inheriting two further properties that make its prompting interface unusually flexible: fine-grained control over individual patches and probabilistic prediction, which allows unspecified content to remain open to multiple plausible continuations. We kindly refer readers to Appendix Sec B.1 for details.

sections.title: 2.3 Reinforcement Learning: Adaptive Stream-of-Thought Reasoning
sections.content: Beyond executing prescribed reasoning pathways, Ψ-0.6 learns representation-adaptive streams of thought choosing which representation to use and when from task feedback. Within the shared token interface, these choices become policy actions, making the reasoning strategy itself target of optimization. We instantiate this approach through reinforcement learning and apply it to visual question answering. The policy selects visual representations, including depth, camera motion, 5 Ψ-0.6: Adaptive Streams of Thought in Unified Vision-Language World Model and optical flow, according to the input and question, and receives reward based on downstream answer quality. Section 6 specifies the learning formulation, training procedure, and evaluation.

sections.title: 2.4 Training Recipe: Pretraining, Mid-training, and Post-training
sections.content: Pretraining builds broad base of predictive knowledge, mid-training integrates additional representations and data, and post-training teaches task-directed use of the resulting capabilities. In each supervised stage, we form different dataset groups (e.g., image captioning, video question answering), each with its own datasets and sequence notations, and allocate training ratio to each. Training on these dataset groups is unified under simple next-token prediction objective. Thus, sequence construction determines both what the model observes and what it learns to predict. Pretraining: visual world modeling and geometric integration. The model is pretrained on large video dataset spanning natural scenes, human activity, and robot interaction. Training begins with RGB and camera conditioning and continues with depth and flow integrated into the sequence. Pure RGB sequences train appearance and motion prediction; interleaved sequences additionally train relationships between images and geometric structure. Keeping both in the mixture exposes the model to prediction with different amounts and types of conditioning information. This stage extends Probabilistic Structure Integration (PSI; Ψ) [14], part of lineage of models demonstrating state-of-the-art visual understanding and world modeling across optical flow and point tracking [18], depth estimation and novel-view synthesis [19], object segmentation [20], physical object discovery and 3D manipulation [21], and perceptual simulation [22]. Ψ-0.6 extends these visual prediction and control capabilities to language-grounded reasoning in subsequent stages. Mid-training: vision-language alignment. The next step is learning language through text-only data from FineWeb-Edu and DataComp-LM (DCLM), followed by vision-language alignment by adding images and videos paired with captions, both global and temporally indexed. Post-training: useful, controllable, user-directed reasoning. Instruction tuning introduces image and video question answering and text-to-video control of camera and object motion. Post-training also teaches spatial reasoning (4) and answering questions by counterfactually imagining object motion (5). Pretraining and mid-training sequences are retained to preserve the models broad predictive capabilities. Beyond these next-token prediction stages, reinforcement learning trains adaptive streams of thought from task feedback, improving how the model selects intermediate representations for downstream reasoning (6).

sections.title: 3 Related Work
sections.content: Unified multimodal models and reasoning. growing line of work unifies increasingly broad sets of modalities and capabilities within single model  (Fig. 3)  . Unified-IO, Unified-IO 2, and 4M-21 cast diverse vision, language, and geometric tasks into shared prediction interfaces [3, 4, 5]. Chameleon and Emu3.5 extend this paradigm to interleaved image and text generation [6, 7]. More recent work uses unified models for multimodal reasoning: ThinkMorph, AD-Loop, and BRAID interleave visual and textual reasoning steps [23, 24, 25], while COOPER incorporates depth and segmentation for spatial reasoning [26]. These works demonstrate that shared multimodal representations can support not only diverse tasks, but also compositional reasoning. Ψ-0.6 builds on these advances by integrating vision-language reasoning with physical world modeling through shared token interface. This enables reasoning through explicit geometry and motion, including counterfactual simulation, while learning to select task-relevant representations from downstream feedback. Tool-augmented LLMs and VLMs. Another line of work enables compositional reasoning by allowing language or vision-language models to invoke external models, tools, or programs [8, 9, 10]  (Fig. 3)  . In contrast, the intermediate operations in Ψ-0.6 are generated by the reasoner itself through the same shared token interface, rather than delegated to separately parameterized systems. This makes both the choice of intermediate representation and its contents part of the models own computation, enabling end-to-end optimization of the reasoning process; we discuss the resulting advantages for co-adaptation, counterfactual generation, and task-dependent intermediate representations in 6.

sections.title: 4 Capability and Compositional Unification: Spatial Intelligence
sections.content: Ψ-0.6 represents our hypothesis for building unified VLMs with capable spatial intelligence. First, we start from visual world model backbone trained to jointly model appearance, geometry, 8 Ψ-0.6: Adaptive Streams of Thought in Unified Vision-Language World Model and motion [14], then extend it with language. Standard VLMs typically attach visual encoder to pretrained LLM, whose initial predictive knowledge comes from text [27, 28]. Language pretraining does not directly supervise how appearance changes with viewpoint or object motion. We hypothesize that learning these relationships through visual and geometric prediction provides stronger foundation for spatial reasoning, with language supplying an interface to these capabilities. Second, we ground reasoning in explicit geometric abstractions, whereas standard VLMs reason and answer primarily in text. single transformer interleaves RGB frames, camera pose, depth, optical flow, point tracks, and text as unified token sequence. These visual streams of thought express spatial structure and motion in intermediate predictions that can be inspected to diagnose errors. Third, unifying world-model and vision-language capabilities yields compositional, endto-end reasoning. Flexible token orderings express pose estimation, novel view synthesis, and question answering, allowing one tasks output to condition the next. spatial question can thus combine capabilities of the same model architecture estimate the camera motion the question describes, get to the view that reveals the answer, then read it. MINDCUBE tests spatial reasoning across multiple views of scene [15]. It is challenging in two ways: (i) its questions involve counterfactual camera motions (e.g., turn left) rather than answering from static images/video, and (ii) its images are separated by large angles (e.g., 90 degrees), which is unlike how most video models and VLMs are trained. MINDCUBE is organized into three categories (Fig. 4A), all requiring integrating observations across large viewpoint changes and reasoning in the reference frame specified by the question. Zero-shot. Frozen Ψ-0.6 reaches 49.751.3% across RGB-only, RGB-depth, and RGB-camera configurations (Fig. 4C). Ψ-0.6 is state-of-the-art relative to open-source generalist VLMs (DeepSeekVL2-Small, LLaVA-OneVision-7B, Qwen3-VL-8B), and spatial specialists (RoboBrain, Space-Qwen, Spatial-MLLM). Compositional Prompting. Beyond directly answering the question, Ψ-0.6 can combine its VLM capabilities with its vision and world-modeling capabilities (Figure 4B). Ψ-0.6 uses inverse dynamics: predict relative camera poses, select the real input view matching the questions requested turn, and read the answer from it. Alternatively, Ψ-0.6 uses novel view synthesis (NVS): generate an RGB frame at the target camera pose and read the answer from this imagined view. Inverse dynamics requires the viewpoint to be one of the inputs, but NVS additionally allows viewpoint absent from the inputs. Using inverse dynamics, Ψ-0.6 reaches 57.7%, compared to 51.3% zero-shot. SFT. MINDCUBE fine-tuning yields 68.7% with RGB-only inputs and 76.3% with RGB+camera inputs on the held-out Tiny test split (Fig. 4C). The RGB-only result exceeds the displayed SFT-only Qwen2.5-VL and 3DThinker baselines. The RGB+camera result exceeds InternVL3s map-thenreason configuration and Qwen2.5-VL with SFT+RL, is comparable to 3DThinker with SFT+RL (76.0%), and trails GeoThinker (83.0%) [15, 29, 30].

William James, The Principles of Psychology Whereas Ψ-0.6 used prescribed reasoning pathways in the previous sections, here we show that it can learn streams of thought that are self-generated, representation-adaptive, and unfold over time. As reasoning proceeds, the model learns not only what intermediate content to generate, but which representation to invoke and when. Unification makes both the choice and generation of these intermediates into actions of the same policy, enabling reinforcement learning on task feedback to optimize the reasoning process end to end (optimization unification). Self-generated intermediates. Unlike tool-augmented LLMs and VLMs that invoke external models or programs [8, 9, 10], Ψ-0.6 generates its intermediates within the reasoner itself. For example, bottle and its cap are one segment for object recognition, yet separate segments for robotic manipulation. Representation-adaptive computation. Ψ-0.6 uses representation-adaptive test-time compute through explicit geometric projections of the world. In text chain-of-thought, the representational medium is fixed language; in Ψ-0.6, the medium itself becomes part of the computation. Unfolds over time. Different representations can be called into computation as the situation evolves: depth for spatial structure, optical flow for motion, camera pose across viewpoints, or predicted scene to imagine what may happen next. This is particularly relevant to embodied agents and robotics, where perception and action unfold continuously in the world. 13 Ψ-0.6: Adaptive Streams of Thought in Unified Vision-Language World Model Learning to Select Streams of Thought Although our framework is generic, here we show proof-of-concept specifically for visual question-answering. Given video and question q, the policy emits notation selecting from depth, camera-motion, and optical-flow streams (Fig. 6A). For example, d0, c23, f23 requests depth at the first frame and camera motion and flow between two later frames. This turns Ψ-0.6s generic prompting interface into policy over reasoning representations. At high level, reinforcement learning alternates between two phases (Fig. 6B): Collect data with the policy. For each question, sample notations from the current policy (initialized with uniform distribution), and score each by how much it lowers the ground truths loss. We build dataset using videos from EgoDex [43], Something-Something v2 (SSv2) [44], PE [45], and OpenVid-1M [46]. Since these datasets provide captions rather than questions, we convert their captions into question-answer pairs (Appendix A.7). Train the policy on the collected data. Initially, we use filtered behavior cloning (rejectionsampling fine-tuning) on the sampled notations that beat RGB-only to teach the model to emit notations; subsequently, we use on-policy GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization) to update the policys LoRA parameters with rewards relative to the other samples in the group, refining which streams it selects. Learned policy generalizes accuracy improvements to unseen benchmarks. The RL-trained policy improves accuracy on held-out examples from the training distributions (a mean relative gain of 5.6% over video-only question answering), with the largest gains on EgoDex, the most challenging dataset. Encouragingly, this suggests that adaptive reasoning may provide greater benefits on harder problems, where additional intermediate computation is most useful. Critically, these gains transfer to four completely unseen benchmarks (a mean relative gain of 9.0%), providing evidence that the learned policy generalizes beyond its training data. Another encouraging signal is the bestof-k performance is substantially higher than single-rollout (Fig. 6C), indicating further headroom for policy optimization. The selected streams are diverse and, in some cases, interpretable; for example, repeated-action questions can elicit sequences of optical-flow predictions, object interactions can combine depth and flow, and observer-motion questions can combine depth with camera motion.

sections.title: 7 Discussion
sections.content: We introduce Ψ-0.6, unified vision-language world model that turns visual, geometric, linguistic, and world-model predictions into composable reasoning operations. Through capability, compositional, and optimization unification, single model can perceive, imagine, reason, and learn which representations to invoke as problem unfolds. Streams of thought support stronger spatial reasoning, counterfactual imagination, and representation-adaptive reasoning learned from task feedback. Importantly, the medium of reasoning need not be fixed: models can learn not only what to predict, but which representation to reason through and when. This opens path toward agents whose reasoning continually reorganizes itself across representations as they learn from embodied experience. More broadly, reinforcement learning over streams of thought could support remarkably general recipe for representation-adaptive reasoning across diverse domains and modalities. Within shared predictive interface, observations in any modality can supply feedback for learning how to reason through others. For example, given video, stream of thought through depth, optical flow, or camera motion could be rewarded by how well it supports predictions of future visual 14 Ψ-0.6: Adaptive Streams of Thought in Unified Vision-Language World Model input. This serves as label-free, task-independent source of reward without human annotations or separate RL environments. Once perception and prediction are part of the reasoner, observations of the world can provide supervision for not only what an embodied agent predicts, but which representation of the physical world to reason through before acting. Extending Ψ-0.6 with actions and proprioception would allow perception, physical reasoning, imagination, and control to become composable operations of single agent.

sections.title: 7.1 Implications for physical reasoning and learning
sections.content: Benefits of geometric representations in stream-of-thought reasoning. First, geometric representations provide an explicit decomposition of the problem. One might ask why such intermediates should be useful when all the information is contained in the original video itself. But the same is true in mathematical reasoning: all the information is contained in the problem statement, yet explicitly producing and using intermediate chains of thought [47] can decompose difficult computation into simpler steps, improving models final output. Geometric representations can play an analogous role for visual reasoning, exposing depth, motion, correspondence, and camera transformation rather than requiring them to be repeatedly inferred from pixels. Empirically, we find that using these intermediates improves both understanding, such as video questionanswering, and fine-grained prediction and control, such as reasoning through optical flow or camera motion. Second, geometric representations can focus learning on the crucial aspects of the physical world. These are lower-dimensional projections that deliberately abstract away incidental visual detail while preserving factors of the environment such as geometry, motion, correspondence, and viewpoint that might generalize beyond the particular objects, scenes, or environments encountered during training. Predicting several such representations from the same experience can also provide form of data augmentation: single video supplies multiple aligned, structured views of the same underlying physical event. Together, these may improve sample efficiency, particularly in regimes where both the quantity and diversity of data are limited [48], such as robotics, biology, or the experimental sciences. Third, these intermediates combine the twin advantages of interpretability and compactness. Thinking with images/video reasons by generating or editing pixels, making intermediate states directly interpretable [49, 50, 51, 52, 53], whereas latent reasoning compresses intermediate computation into continuous representations that are difficult to inspect directly [54, 55, 56, 57, 58]. Ψ-0.6 occupies middle ground by externalizing compact intermediates as physically meaningful tokens: their semantics are grounded in recognizable properties of the physical world, but they need not reproduce every visual detail to expose the structure relevant to computation.

sections.title: 7.2 Limitations
sections.content: Scale. Our results establish the conceptual and functional consequences of unifying vision, language, and world modeling, rather than exhaust the performance achievable by this framework. Ψ-0.6 was developed at substantially smaller scale in training data, compute, research, and engineering effort than contemporary frontier multi-modal systems. We expect scaling these resources will strengthen all of Ψ-0.6s capabilities; our preliminary experiments already suggest continued gains with scale, motivating further study. 15 Ψ-0.6: Adaptive Streams of Thought in Unified Vision-Language World Model Learning synergy and specialization. Ψ-0.6 advances the broader trend toward unified models by bringing vision, language, and world modeling into shared reasoning process. Unification can promote positive transfer through shared knowledge [59], but can also introduce interference when capabilities compete for limited capacity or require conflicting computations [60, 61, 62]. Ψ-0.6 demonstrates functional unification and inference-time gains from composing capabilities, but we do not isolate positive and negative transfer among those capabilities during training. natural next step is sparse mixture-of-experts architecture, which could retain the advantages of unification while managing the cost of large model [63, 64]. By activating only subset of experts per token, it allows specialization and greater total capacity without proportional increase in inference computation.

sections.title: 7.3 Key open problems
sections.content: From visual proxy actions to embodied control. Our next step is extending the framework from reasoning about actions to acting in the physical world. In Ψ-0.6, optical flow and point tracks already function as proxy actions: they specify how parts of visual scene should move, but do not directly actuate the world. One route toward robotics would be to train an inverse-kinematics (IK) model conditioned on flow or point predictions, analogous to RGB-based IK models [65, 66, 67]. More generally, robot joint commands, end-effector poses, gripper states, and other control signals could become additional token modalities. Policy prediction and world simulation could then become different queries to the same model, extending the unified interface from perception and imagination to physical control. Combining such action tokens with adaptive streams of thought would enable richer form of embodied reasoning. Rather than mapping observations directly to commands, the model could learn when to inspect geometry, predict motion, imagine the consequences of an action, evaluate progress, seek another observation, or act. Our current adaptive-stream experiments optimize downstream task performance on visual question answering rather than physical control. In an embodied agent, reward could jointly optimize what action to take, what reasoning to perform before acting, and how much computation that reasoning should consume. This would extend our adaptive streams of thought from choosing how to reason about the world to choosing how to reason and act within it. Generic verification for the physical world. Physical reasoning may provide an unusually rich source of supervision because different representations of the same world must satisfy shared constraints. Depth, camera motion, optical flow, point tracks, and appearance should agree across viewpoints and time, while forward and inverse predictions create additional cycles that can be checked. For example, camera motion inferred from two views should generate compatible second view when supplied back to the model. Recent work shows that cross-modal cycle consistency can itself provide dense, label-free reward for multimodal reasoning [68]. Such signals suggest route toward generic physical verifiers: mechanisms that score intermediate reasoning through consistency with the structure of the world rather than requiring human labels for every trajectory. Autodiscovery. Verification could, in turn, support an automatic loop for the discovery of reasoning intermediates. Ψ-0.6 currently reasons through deliberately chosen abstractions whose physical meaning is known in advance. Adaptive streams of thought learn which of these representations to 16 Ψ-0.6: Adaptive Streams of Thought in Unified Vision-Language World Model use and when; future systems could instead ask which intermediate representations should exist at all. model could propose compact intermediate variables, evaluate whether reasoning through them improves predictive consistency or downstream task performance [69], and retain useful abstractions within its own reasoning interface. Work on latent-action world models already shows that useful transition representations can emerge from unlabeled video rather than being specified priori [70, 71]. Extending this idea from action representations to reasoning representations suggests closed loop: propose an abstraction, evaluate the consequences of using it, and reincorporate successful abstractions into future computation. In this view, not only the reasoning policy, but the vocabulary through which model reasons, can itself become an object of learning.

MINDCUBE separates in-place camera turns (Rotation), movement around scene (Around), and relative object positions across views (Among; Fig. 4A). Direct RGB+depth prompting is strongest on Around and near chance on Rotation. Structured prompting improves the displayed Rotation and Among results most. The SFT configuration is strong on Around and Among but remains near chance on Rotation we hypothesize that this is because the Rotation training data contains very limited scene diversity, making it challenging for learning to generalize to the test set. Inference protocol for the fine-tuned models. All fine-tuned Ψ-0.6 results on MINDCUBE (Fig. 4C) use direct answering: the model emits the answer immediately after the inputs, without generating text reasoning trace. We fine-tune on the 10k MINDCUBE training questions which are disjoint from the 1,050-question Tiny split used for evaluation mixed with the models general training data. Each training sequence places the question and its answer options first, then the input views (optionally with depth and/or relative camera poses), and ends with the answer. A.2 Details of FlowBench FLOWBENCH [16] is robotics and computer vision benchmark that evaluates the capability of visual world models to answer questions based on specified counterfactual motions. FLOWBENCH contains diverse categories of questions, such as occlusion (if we move the table 0.50 meters to the right, will it occlude the view of the chair?) and closer to (if we move the eraser 5cm to the left, which three objects would it be closest to?). FLOWBENCH contains two main splits. First, FLOWBENCH-SIM is built in simulator [32, 33] and contains diverse indoor scenes with full rooms depicted, and involves moving objects with various scales from chairs to potatoes. Second, FLOWBENCH-REAL was built by adding counterfactual motion questions to five robot datasets: DROID, Bridge V2, Language-Table, RT-1, and Berkeley UR5. It spans five distinct robot embodiments, with scenes ranging from laboratory tabletops to toy kitchens and kitchen counters, and moved objects ranging from colored blocks and toy food to cups, bowls, bottles, utensils, and cloths. sections.title: B Supplementary Text
sections.content: B.1 Preliminaries on Probabilistic Structure Integration (PSI) Ψ-0.6 builds on Probabilistic Structure Integration (PSI) [14], inheriting two further properties that make its prompting interface unusually flexible: fine-grained control over individual patches and probabilistic prediction, which allows unspecified content to remain open to multiple plausible continuations. Fine-grained control. Ψ-0.6 represents visual fields as independently encoded spatial patches, using local patch quantization together with explicit pointer tokens. Each RGB, flow, or depth patch is represented by content tokens describing what the patch contains and pointer token specifying its modality, spatial location, and temporal locationthat is, where and when the content belongs. Because content and location are represented separately, prompt can address only selected regions of visual field, leave the remaining regions unspecified, or relocate existing content by changing its pointer while preserving its content tokens. This enables fine-grained conditioning and targeted scene edits. For example, in Fig. 2B, moving patch on the upper part of can downward while keeping the base fixed specifies compression, whereas moving it upward without fixing the base specifies lift. The same representation also allows patches to be generated in arbitrary spatial order, including sequentially (autoregressively), in parallel, or through combination of both. Probabilistic prediction. Prompts specify constraints rather than single deterministic target. For any partially specified scene, Ψ-0.6 represents distribution over compatible continuations, allowing the same prompt to yield alternative predictions through sampling. B.2 Supplementary Discussion Unifying reasoning and imagination. The value of unified predictive model becomes particularly clear when reasoning requires considering world that has not yet been observed. growing line of work augments language-based reasoners with external visual generators or world models. Mindjourney [83] invokes frozen Stable Virtual Camera [84]; SandboxVLM introduces expert models and 3D reconstruction [85]; Thinking with Novel Views [86] uses an external Painter; APC [87] chains multiple foundation models; and AVIC [88] learns when to invoke world model. These approaches demonstrate the value of visual imagination, but retain separation between the system that reasons and the system that imagines. World2VLM [89] finds benefits from distilling imagined experience into VLM rather than relying only on runtime coupling. Ψ-0.6 pushes this integration further: the model that interprets an observation is also the model that predicts its geometry, motion, and possible transformations. Imagined states are generated and consumed within the same model and token interface as the rest of the reasoning process. When the reasoner and the imaginer are the same model, imagination becomes first-class reasoning operation rather than separately invoked tool. 29 Ψ-0.6: Adaptive Streams of Thought in Unified Vision-Language World Model

sections.title: C Model and Training Details for Reproducibility
sections.content: We describe the implementation of the unified model, its prompting interface, the training of the stream-selection policy, and the supervised training recipe, following the organization of 2. The model inherits the patch-based representation and conditional-prediction approach of PSI [14]; here we specify the tokenization, transformer, sequence construction, and optimization needed to implement these mechanisms. The base recipe describes Ψ-0.6 after approximately 1.2 million supervised training steps, followed by context-length extension. The initialization of the streamselection policy and its answer scorer is described in C.3. C.1 Unified Multimodal Model C.1.1 common token and position interface Each sequence element represents one image, depth map, an optical-flow field, relative camera pose, or text segment. We serialize elements into stream of discrete token IDs. Each token also carries position (x, y, t, c): two spatial coordinates, temporal index, and channel specifying the representation and, where applicable, its code component. The transformer input is the sum of token embedding and channel embedding. Spatial and temporal positions enter attention through rotary embeddings. For visual patch, serialization emits fixed pointer token followed by the patchs content codes. The pointer has token ID 65,000; its position identifies the requested patch, and its channel is the first content channel of that modality. The same pointer ID is reused across locations and modalities. Pointers supply the location as conditioning information, and prediction loss is applied to the supervised content codes. The transformer has one 65,536-entry token embedding and output vocabulary. Code indices overlap across modalities: for example, visual code and text token can have the same integer ID, with their channel embeddings distinguishing their roles. Learned codes for normalized inverse depth on the same patch grid. Learned codes for two-dimensional displacement; channels also encode the temporal gap. Two fields of view, three axisangle rotation components, and three translation components. GPT-2 byte-pair encoding, followed by an end-of-text token. Table 5: Token representations. Pointer tokens count toward sequence length but do not receive prediction loss. Patch sizes are in image pixels, whereas the models spatial coordinates index the patch grid. 30 Ψ-0.6: Adaptive Streams of Thought in Unified Vision-Language World Model C.1.2 Visual quantization and geometric labels Local patch codes. RGB, depth, and flow use separately trained, frozen patch quantizers. Their encoders apply Haar wavelet transform within each 16 16 patch, project the patch to 512 features, and process it with three residual blocks using 11 convolutions. Each residual block uses channel-wise layer normalization (LayerNorm, ϵ = 105), hidden width of 1,024, and sigmoid linear unit (SiLU) activations. Encoding is therefore local to each patch. Finite scalar quantization (FSQ) maps six scalar components, with (8, 8, 8, 5, 5, 5) levels, to one of 8353 = 64, 000 discrete indices. Quantizer training uses straight-through estimator (STE) for rounding. There are four such codes per RGB patch and two per depth or flow patch. The first code has an auxiliary coarse-reconstruction objective. Decoders use nine residual blocks with 33 convolutions on the code grid followed by an inverse Haar wavelet transform, so reconstruction can combine information across neighboring patches. The RGB quantizer was trained on ImageNet and OpenImages with an L1 reconstruction term, DINOv2 feature term, and coarse L1 term weighted by 0.01. The flow quantizer uses squared reconstruction error and coarse squared error term weighted by 0.01. These quantizers are trained independently and frozen during autoregressive transformer training, which uses precomputed visual codes. Depth and camera geometry. The corpus preprocessing pipeline uses Depth Anything 3 (DA3) to estimate depth, camera intrinsics, and camera poses from video. Depth is converted to inverse depth, normalized to clips inverse-depth range, and quantized as three-channel replicated scalar image. Reconstruction uses the stored per-clip normalization bounds to convert decoded values back to depth. Optical flow. The flow preprocessing pipeline estimates displacement with AllTracker in two-frame mode. Horizontal and vertical displacement are expressed in pixels at the preprocessing resolution, divided by 40 before quantization, and multiplied by 40 after decoding. Each stored field has an associated frame gap. Training sequences use only frame pairs for which the required flow field is available. Flow positions carry the source time, while gap-dependent pair of channels distinguishes the two content codes and the temporal interval. Camera-pose discretization. Given camera-to-world matrices Ti and Tj, the camera element represents 1 Tj. Horizontal and vertical fields of view are rounded to integer degrees. The rotation is expressed as three-component axisangle vector in degrees; each component is clipped to [180, 180], rounded, and shifted by 180. Translation components are expressed in centimeters, clipped to [1000, 1000], rounded, and shifted by 1000. This deterministic discretization produces eight integers occupying fixed component channels. The sequence notation identifies the source and destination frames; camera tokens use spatial coordinates (0, 0) and the source frames temporal coordinate. To use the same spatial-position interface as visual tokens, text is laid out in rows of width 100: token position has = mod 100 and = k/100. Its temporal index associates the segment with frame or clip. C.1.4 Transformer architecture The model is decoder-only transformer with approximately 8.05 billion parameters. Each block uses pre-norm layout, applying root mean square normalization (RMSNorm) before grouped-query attention (GQA) with causal mask and before Swish-gated linear unit (SwiGLU) feed-forward network, with residual connections around both operations. C.2 Generic Prompting Interface: Streams-of-Thought C.2.1 Notation and sequence construction notation lists the elements of sequence in causal order. Node elements refer to one time index, as in RGB0 or D0; edge elements refer to pair, as in C01 or F01. Here D, C, and denote depth, relative camera pose, and optical flow, respectively. At inference, an arrow separates supplied context from requested outputs. For example, RGB0, C01 RGB1 requests new image conditioned on source image and camera motion, whereas RGB0, RGB1 C01 requests the relative camera pose. Longer streams concatenate these operations, making generated content available to later predictions. Training uses complete sequences sampled from finite, weighted set of notations for each dataset group. The temporal sampler maps the notations indices to available frames and geometric edges in clip. Each element is then loaded, allocated token budget, and serialized. Examples from the instruction mixture include RGB0, C01, F01, RGB1 for geometric video modeling; RGB0, D0, T0 for image description; and Q, RGB0, D0, for answering an image question with depth, where T0 is caption and and are question and answer text. Video-question sequences can place the question before or after the images, and geometric representations can be interleaved with images 32 Ψ-0.6: Adaptive Streams of Thought in Unified Vision-Language World Model or placed between the question and answer. Token allocation and patch order. During base training, the 4,096-token budget includes pointers and conditioning tokens. Text and fixed-length camera elements are accounted for first. The remaining budget is distributed approximately uniformly in patch count across image, depth, and flow elements, subject to their available patch counts. The allocator accounts for five tokens per RGB patch and three per depth or flow patch, with stochastic remainder allocation and final length adjustment to meet the sequence budget. Within each visual element, patches are randomly permuted and the allocated subset is retained; text retains its linguistic order. Short sequences are padded with masked positions. Element selection and supervision. Sampling different notations exposes the model to different conditioning sets and prediction orders. Each dataset groups loss mask specifies the conditioning elements and supervised targets. The first RGB element usually serves as context; the final global-caption group also supervises it, supporting text-first image prediction. Question-answer groups supervise answer text, with their image, depth, flow, pose, and question tokens providing context. The group masks and mixture weights are described in C.4. C.2.2 Generating and composing elements Generation begins by serializing the supplied elements and constructing template for the requested element. The template supplies pointer tokens, positions, and channels, while leaving content slots to be sampled from the transformers output distribution. Content IDs are sampled within the configured range of the target modality. The resulting codes can be retained as context for the next element or decoded into visual representation. To accelerate visual inference, the decoder combines an autoregressive patch prefix with parallel decoding of the remaining patches. It first generates chosen number of patches sequentially, caching attention keys and values to establish shared structure. The remaining patches are processed concurrently, with content codes within each patch generated sequentially. Each parallel patch attends to the supplied context, the completed prefix, and its own preceding content codes. This reduces the number of sequential decoding steps needed to complete visual output. The sequential budget is measured in patches. Temperature, top-k, nucleus threshold, patch ordering, and sequential patch budget control inference. Generic generation defaults to temperature 1, top-k 1,000, nucleus threshold 1, and 32 sequential patches.
